title: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights

slides.title: Which court
slides.text: Under Article 256(1) TFEU and Article 51 of the Statute: applications by Union institutions and member states go to the Court of Justice; applications by natural and legal persons go to the General Court.

cards.q: Where does a company bring an action for annulment, and where does a member state?
cards.a: A natural or legal person brings it before the General Court; a member state or Union institution before the Court of Justice (Art 256(1) TFEU, Art 51 Statute).

slides.title: The four admissibility requirements
slides.text: A checklist to run in order for every annulment problem. There must be a LEGALLY BINDING EU ACT. The applicant and defendant must have STANDING. There must be a LEGAL INTEREST. And the action must be brought within TWO MONTHS. Most exam cases are decided on the second.

cards.q: What must be checked for the admissibility of an action for annulment?
cards.a: A legally binding EU act; standing of applicant and defendant; a legal interest; and the two-month time limit.

slides.title: Three classes of applicant
slides.text: FULLY PRIVILEGED: member states, Parliament, Council, Commission — they may challenge any act without showing anything further. SEMI-PRIVILEGED: Court of Auditors, ECB, Committee of the Regions — only for the purpose of protecting their own prerogatives. NON-PRIVILEGED: everyone else, in particular natural and legal persons under the law of a member state, public entities not acting as a member state as such (provinces, municipalities, public associations), and EU bodies not otherwise listed such as the Economic and Social Committee, the European Council and the EIB. The defendant is always an EU entity capable of imposing obligations.

cards.q: Distinguish fully privileged, semi-privileged and non-privileged applicants in annulment actions.
cards.a: Fully privileged (member states, Parliament, Council, Commission) need show nothing further. Semi-privileged (Court of Auditors, ECB, Committee of the Regions) may act only to protect their own prerogatives. Non-privileged applicants — everyone else, including individuals and companies — must satisfy Article 263(4).

cards.q: A German Land wants to annul a Commission decision. Which class of applicant is it?
cards.a: Non-privileged. A public entity that does not act as the member state as such — a province, municipality or public association — is treated like any other legal person and must satisfy Article 263(4).

slides.title: Article 263(4): the three gateways
slides.text: A non-privileged applicant gets in through one of three doors. (1) They are the ADDRESSEE of the act. (2) The act is of DIRECT AND INDIVIDUAL CONCERN to them. (3) The act is a REGULATORY ACT of direct concern to them which does not entail implementing measures. The third gateway was added by Lisbon precisely because the second is so hard to pass.

cards.q: State the three alternatives under Article 263(4) TFEU for a non-privileged applicant.
cards.a: Being the addressee of the act; direct AND individual concern; or a regulatory act of direct concern not entailing implementing measures.

slides.title: Gateway 1: addressee
slides.text: The easy case — for example an undertaking that is the addressee of a Commission competition decision.

slides.title: Gateway 2: direct and individual concern
slides.text: DIRECT concern: the act affects the applicant immediately and in fact, rather than having its legal effects depend on further, uncertain events — in practice, no discretion left to the implementing authority. INDIVIDUAL concern is the Plaumann formula (Case 25/62): the act must affect them by reason of certain attributes PECULIAR TO THEM, or by circumstances differentiating them from all other persons, so as to distinguish them individually just as in the case of an addressee. The formula is notoriously restrictive: anyone who could in principle join the affected group later is not individually concerned.

terms.def: Individual concern requires attributes peculiar to the applicant or circumstances differentiating them from all others as if they were an addressee.

cards.q: State the Plaumann test for individual concern.
cards.a: The act must affect the applicant by reason of attributes peculiar to them, or circumstances differentiating them from all other persons, so as to distinguish them individually just as in the case of the addressee (Case 25/62).

cards.q: Why does the Plaumann test so rarely admit individual applicants?
cards.a: Because if the affected category is open — anyone could in principle enter the trade or activity later — the applicant is affected only as a member of a general class and so is not differentiated from all other persons.

slides.title: When individual concern does succeed
slides.text: Three recognised categories. A CLOSED CLASS: the act affects a distinct and definite group, fixed at the moment of adoption. PARTICIPATION in the procedure leading to the act. And infringement of SPECIFIC RIGHTS, such as trademark rights, or a noticeable disadvantage to the applicant's market position — the classic example being a direct competitor challenging a state aid decision.

cards.q: Give three situations in which an applicant is individually concerned.
cards.a: A closed class fixed at adoption; participation in the procedure leading to the act; and infringement of specific rights or a noticeable disadvantage to the applicant's market position — for instance a competitor challenging state aid.

slides.title: Gateway 3: regulatory acts
slides.text: Direct concern as above, plus a 'regulatory act' as defined in Inuit (C-583/11 P): it is NOT a legislative act — so it means tertiary or administrative acts; it has general and abstract scope; and it does not require further implementing measures. The Court's reading disappointed those who hoped Lisbon had opened standing: legislative acts remain subject to the full Plaumann test.

terms.def: A non-legislative act of general application — tertiary or administrative — Inuit (C-583/11 P).

cards.q: What is a 'regulatory act' under Article 263(4) TFEU after Inuit?
cards.a: A non-legislative act — tertiary or administrative — of general and abstract scope that does not entail implementing measures. Legislative acts fall outside, so challenging them still requires individual concern under Plaumann.

slides.title: The effect of annulment
slides.text: Cassation. The contested act and its legal effects are repealed EX TUNC — as if it had never existed — unless the Court exceptionally upholds certain effects, which it does to protect legal certainty. And the judgment has ERGA OMNES effect: the act ceases to exist for everyone, including third parties, not merely between the litigants.

cards.q: What is the effect of a successful action for annulment?
cards.a: The act is repealed ex tunc, with erga omnes effect — it ceases to exist for everyone — unless the Court exceptionally maintains some of its effects for legal certainty.

slides.title: Section: action for failure to act (Art 265 TFEU)
The requirements
slides.text: The mirror image of annulment: a legally binding EU act that should have been adopted; standing of applicant and defendant; legal interest; and a time limit of TWO MONTHS SINCE THE REQUEST. The request is the key step — the institution must first be called upon to act, and only its failure to define its position within two months opens the action.

cards.q: What must happen before an action for failure to act can be brought?
cards.a: The institution must first be called upon to act; only if it fails to define its position within two months of being so requested does the action lie (Art 265 TFEU).

slides.title: Standing differs from annulment
slides.text: Two differences worth noting. There is NO distinction between privileged and semi-privileged applicants — all member states and institutions are fully privileged here. And for non-privileged applicants, direct and individual concern arises from the failure to ADDRESS AN ACT TO THEM, which is a narrower gateway than under Article 263.

cards.q: How does standing under Article 265 TFEU differ from Article 263?
cards.a: All member states and institutions are fully privileged under Art 265 — the semi-privileged category disappears. Non-privileged applicants must show that the institution failed to address an act TO THEM.

slides.title: The judgment and what follows
slides.text: The Court makes a DECLARATION that the failure was unlawful; it does not itself adopt the missing act. And the finding may give rise to the Union's tortious liability under Article 340 TFEU — to be pursued SEPARATELY through an action for damages under Article 268 TFEU.

cards.q: Does the Court adopt the missing measure when it upholds an action for failure to act?
cards.a: No — it declares the failure unlawful. The institution must then act; and the finding may found a separate damages claim against the Union under Arts 340 and 268 TFEU.

slides.title: The early stage
slides.text: There was no codified fundamental rights instrument, and in cases 36/59 and following — Ruhrkohlenverkaufsgesellschaften — the Court treated fundamental rights as a matter of MEMBER STATE law, outside its remit. The member state reaction was Solange I. And the underlying problem is stated exactly on the slide: with direct effect and primacy, supranational law reached individuals directly while offering them no rights protection — a deficit of legal protection.

cards.q: Why did the absence of EU fundamental rights become a problem only after direct effect and primacy?
cards.a: Because those doctrines made EU law apply to individuals directly and override national protections — so national fundamental rights could no longer shield them, and EU law offered nothing in their place.

slides.title: The intermediate stage
slides.text: Still no codified instrument, but in Internationale Handelsgesellschaft (11/70) the Court recognised fundamental rights as GENERAL PRINCIPLES of EU law, drawn from the constitutional traditions common to the member states and from the ECHR. The member state response was Solange II: as long as EU protection remains sufficient, the German court will not exercise its own review. Judicial dialogue produced the protection the Treaties lacked.

slides.title: Can the EU accede to the ECHR?
slides.text: Article 6(2) TEU makes accession a political objective — and the Court of Justice has rejected it TWICE, in Opinion 2/94 and Opinion 2/13. The main objection is the AUTONOMY of EU law: accession would let the ECHR and the case law of the Strasbourg Court take precedence over both EU primary law and the Court of Justice's own jurisprudence. Note the irony worth a sentence in an essay: the Court insists on fundamental rights protection but resists external review of its own compliance.

cards.q: Why has the Court of Justice blocked EU accession to the ECHR?
cards.a: To protect the autonomy of EU law: accession would subject EU primary law and the Court's own case law to the ECHR and the Strasbourg Court (Opinions 2/94 and 2/13), even though Article 6(2) TEU makes accession an objective.

slides.title: The current stage
slides.text: The Charter of Fundamental Rights, drawn up by a Convention in 2000 during the constitutionalisation process, became a binding part of PRIMARY LAW with the Treaty of Lisbon in 2009.

slides.title: Two bases today
slides.text: Fundamental rights protection now rests on two pillars simultaneously. GENERAL PRINCIPLES of Union law under Article 6(3) TEU, drawn from the ECHR and the constitutional traditions of the member states. And the CHARTER, which is primary law. The general principles did not disappear when the Charter became binding — they still cover what the Charter does not.

cards.q: On what two bases does EU fundamental rights protection rest today?
cards.a: The Charter of Fundamental Rights, which is primary law since Lisbon, and the general principles of Union law under Article 6(3) TEU, drawn from the ECHR and the member states' common constitutional traditions.

slides.title: Three generations of rights in the Charter
slides.text: Liberal and political rights of the FIRST generation: human dignity, freedoms, equality. Fundamental SOCIAL rights of the second: employment services, social security. And COLLECTIVE rights of the third: environmental protection. The Charter's inclusion of the second and third generations is what distinguishes it from the ECHR.

slides.title: Who holds Charter rights
slides.text: Natural persons — though some rights belong only to Union citizens, such as the right to vote or, as the slide has it, rights tied to citizenship. And legal persons, EXCEPT for highly personal rights such as human dignity and the right to life, which a company cannot hold.

cards.q: Can a company invoke the Charter?
cards.a: Yes, for rights capable of applying to legal persons — but not for highly personal rights such as human dignity or the right to life. Some rights are also reserved to Union citizens.

slides.title: Who is bound: Article 51(1)
slides.text: The institutions, bodies, offices and agencies of the Union — always. And the MEMBER STATES ONLY WHEN IMPLEMENTING UNION LAW, which Åkerberg Fransson (C-617/10) read broadly as 'in all cases governed by Union law', that is within the scope of EU law. Whether PRIVATE PARTIES are bound is the open question, raised by Bauer (C-569/16 and C-570/16), where a Charter right was applied in a dispute between private persons. In a case, always establish first that the situation falls within the scope of EU law — without that, the Charter does not apply at all.

terms.def: The Charter binds the Union institutions always, and the member states only when implementing Union law.

cards.q: A national measure allegedly breaches a Charter right. What must be established before the Charter can be applied?
cards.a: That the member state was implementing Union law — read in Åkerberg Fransson as any situation governed by EU law, i.e. within its scope. Outside that scope the Charter does not bind the member state at all.

cards.q: Can the Charter be invoked between private parties?
cards.a: Contested but increasingly yes for certain provisions — Bauer (C-569/16, C-570/16) applied a Charter right in a dispute between private persons, on the same logic as the Mangold line.
